author: claire-harmon
title: It's 3 a.m. Again: Your Anxiety Isn't Imagined
dek: Why perimenopause can set off your brain's alarm system out of nowhere, and why it was never a character flaw.
seo_title: 3 a.m. Anxiety in Perimenopause: It's Not All in Your Head
seo_description: Why perimenopause can set off your brain's alarm system in the middle of the night, and why it was never a character flaw.
pull_quote: You didn't lose your ability to cope. You lost the steady hormones that were helping you cope.
body_html:
It's 3 a.m. Your heart is hammering. You're lying in the dark, running through every possible reason: the 2 p.m. coffee, the odd email from your boss, something you said to your sister three weeks ago.

You are exhausted. Your mind will not stop.

By morning you've reached the usual verdict: something is wrong with me. Maybe you've even been told it's stress, and that you should try to worry less. (Helpful.)

Here's what I wish someone had told me sooner. You are not falling apart, and you are not suddenly fragile. What's happening may well have a biological explanation. You are not just in your head. You may be in perimenopause.

Your brain's calming system is tuned by your hormones

Think of GABA as your brain's volume knob for fear. When the amygdala, your brain's alarm center, starts firing, GABA steps in and turns the signal down. We're safe. Stand down.

Your hormones help tune that system. And in perimenopause, estrogen doesn't decline in a tidy straight line. It fluctuates: high one week, low the next. One research team has proposed that those swings can unsettle this calming chemistry in some women, leaving your alarm system with less buffering (Gordon et al., 2015). A racing heart at 3 a.m. may be part of that picture.

Then there's progesterone, the part most women never hear about. Your body converts progesterone into a compound called allopregnanolone, which acts on those same GABA receptors and has a strong calming effect. It is, in effect, one of your body's own built-in anti-anxiety compounds. When progesterone drops, there's less raw material for that calming signal.

You didn't suddenly get bad at life. You didn't lose your ability to cope. You lost the steady hormones that were helping you cope.

You didn't lose your ability to cope. You lost the steady hormones that were helping you cope.

Why a Tuesday email now feels like an emergency

There's a third player: cortisol, your main stress hormone. Your ovarian hormones help regulate the HPA axis, the control tower that decides when to release cortisol and, crucially, when to call it back. Perimenopause may disrupt that calibration.

Researchers are still working out how this plays out. In one small pilot study of 15 perimenopausal women, those with bigger estrogen swings had a higher heart rate during a lab stress test and felt more rejection, anger and sadness, though their cortisol wasn't higher (Gordon et al., 2019). Same life. Same stressor. For some women, a bigger alarm.

Your body isn't overreacting. It may be working with less of its usual regulation. That difference matters, because it means the answer isn't trying harder to think calm thoughts. It's working with your nervous system, giving it signals it's no longer getting from steady hormones.

And if a doctor brushed this off as "just stress," that's worth a second conversation, ideally with someone who takes the hormonal side seriously. You are allowed to bring notes.

A small practice for tonight

Start building your own evidence. Grab a notebook and answer these, one per sitting if brain fog is loud today:

  • When did you first notice this anxiety, or notice it getting worse? A rough age or year is fine.
  • Does it follow any pattern in your cycle, or does it seem random?
  • What does it feel like in your body, before any thought shows up? Racing heart, tight chest, a drop in your stomach?

There's no right answer. You're drawing the first lines of a map, and that map makes the next doctor's visit a very different conversation.

The Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, where this chapter lives in full, is coming soon.
source: The Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, Chapter 1: Your Anxiety Is Not in Your Head

author: claire-harmon
title: The Physiological Sigh: Calm in 90 Seconds
dek: A two-breath tool for sudden perimenopause anxiety that works in a meeting, in the car, or at 3 a.m.
seo_title: The Physiological Sigh: A Breathing Exercise to Calm Down
seo_description: Two inhales and one long exhale: a breathing exercise to calm down during sudden perimenopause anxiety, in a meeting, in the car or at 3 a.m.
pull_quote: The exhale is where the calm lives.
body_html:
It's 2:47 on a Wednesday afternoon and you're in a meeting. Nothing dramatic is happening. And yet your chest tightens, your thoughts speed up, and you're suddenly sure you're about to cry, flee, or say something you'll regret.

This is perimenopause anxiety in its daytime outfit. And it often arrives when you can't exactly lie down on the conference room floor.

So here's the tool I reach for first. It takes about a minute, needs no equipment, and nobody around you will notice.

Why a breath can help

It's called the physiological sigh: two inhales stacked on top of each other, then one long, slow exhale. In a small, month-long randomized study at Stanford (Balban et al., 2023), people spent five minutes a day on one of three breathing patterns or on mindfulness meditation. Anxiety eased after practice in every group, with no clear winner. The people doing the sigh had a bigger lift in mood than the meditators, and a bigger drop in their breathing rate. The practice below is a shorter version of what they did.

The idea is refreshingly simple. Your body already sighs on its own every few minutes, partly to re-inflate the tiny air sacs in your lungs (Li et al., 2016). The second little inhale fills your lungs a bit more, which makes room for a longer exhale. And your heart rate naturally slows as you breathe out, which researchers think may be part of why long exhales feel calming.

The exhale is where the calm lives. In perimenopause, when your hormones are shifting, your body can seem to stay in alarm mode longer than the moment deserves. The sigh is one small way to step out of that loop. You're not thinking your way out. You're breathing your way out.

The exhale is where the calm lives.

The practice

Safety note: if you have asthma or any condition affecting your breathing, check with your doctor before changing your breathing pattern. You can return to normal breathing at any point.

Sit or stand comfortably. This takes one to two minutes.

  1. Take a full, normal inhale through your nose. (Count to 3.)
  2. Without exhaling, take one more quick sniff through your nose, stacking it on top of the first breath. (One second. Your lungs will feel full.)
  3. Open your mouth slightly. Exhale slowly and completely, letting all the air out. (Count to 6 or 8. Longer than feels natural.)
  4. Pause at the bottom of the exhale for one or two counts before your next breath.
  5. Repeat 2 to 4 times, then return to normal breathing.

What you might notice: a big involuntary sigh or yawn (good sign), a bit of lightheadedness after the first round (if it doesn't pass quickly, stop and breathe normally), warmth in your chest or shoulders. Or nothing dramatic at all, which is also completely normal. Regulation is often quiet at first.

If the double inhale feels uncomfortable, try one deep inhale for 4 counts and a long exhale for 8. If you feel dizzy, open your eyes, look around the room, and name three things you can see before continuing.

Your 90 seconds this week

Pick one predictable moment, like the mid-afternoon slump when brain fog peaks and anxiety quietly rises. Before you reach for your phone or another coffee, do two physiological sighs. Then notice what your body does. No transformation required. Just 90 seconds of evidence.

This tool, and the rest of the 10-minute calm toolkit, is in The Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, coming soon.
source: The Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, Chapter 3: The 10-Minute Calm Toolkit (Tool 1)
